curation.lead:
Alessandro Benedetti (born July 1961) is a Geneva-based Italian financier, founding partner of Schwarzfield, and CEO of SAE Capital Ltd, who operated as Jeffrey Epstein’s neighbor on Avenue Foch in Paris from at least December 2011. In a candid email that month, Reid Weingarten asked Epstein: “did we ever talk about allesandro Benedetti, your Italian jewish neighbor on ave. foch?” (EFTA00925685). Epstein ignored the question in writing, deflecting to scheduling — a pattern suggesting either a phone conversation or a deliberate preference not to discuss Benedetti on record. Through September and October 2013, Epstein’s assistant Lesley Groff sent multiple reminders tagged “Allesandro de Benedetti-Paris” (EFTA02575276, EFTA02576024), and Benedetti appeared first on Epstein’s “Paris List” of contacts (EFTA02575400) alongside Ariane de Rothschild, Wojtek Fibak, and a “Sultan.” That same September 26 schedule placed Benedetti in the orbit of an Ian Osborne breakfast, a Larry Summers lunch, and a meeting with Richard Kahn and Darren Indyke before Epstein departed for Paris via Air France.

Benedetti’s independent career centers on high-stakes cross-border dealmaking. His signature transaction was brokering the 2005 acquisition of Wind Telecomunicazioni SpA for Egyptian billionaire Naguib Sawiris — at approximately €12 billion, then the largest leveraged buyout in European history. Benedetti received over €67 million in fees but sued Sawiris for a one-third ownership stake, losing at the UK Supreme Court in July 2013 (Benedetti v Sawiris). He was separately investigated by Roman prosecutors in 2008 for corruption related to the Wind deal. His corporate portfolio spans jurisdictions: Attali Investment Partners Ltd (UK, 2010–2015) with former Mitterrand adviser Jacques Attali; Asherco LLP (UK, 2012–present) with rotating BVI corporate members; SPQR Capital Holdings S.A.; Schwarzfield S.A.; and the NYSE-listed Equus Total Return Inc., where he served as Executive Chairman from 2011 to 2014 (SEC EDGAR CIK 878932). Through the ICIJ Paradise Papers, he is confirmed as a shareholder of Tree of Life Limited (Malta, C67345), with a registered address in Florence.

In January 2015, SoftBank executive Rajeev Misra hired Benedetti to run a covert sabotage campaign against internal rivals Nikesh Arora and Alok Sama. Misra paid $500,000 through Standard Chartered Bank to Barkmere Group Ltd, a BVI entity controlled by Benedetti. The operation involved a failed honey trap in Tokyo using women and hidden cameras, subcontracting Nicolas Giannakopoulos (a Swiss operative with Cambridge Analytica/SCL Group ties) to distribute leaked banking records and run a shareholder pressure campaign. Bertrand des Pallieres, a former Deutsche Bank trader who had worked under Misra, made the introduction. When Misra failed to deliver Benedetti’s expected compensation — a cut of SoftBank earnings and the leadership of the Vision Fund’s London office — Benedetti leaked the entire operation to the Wall Street Journal, which published its exposé in February 2020. Critically, on January 28, 2019, just two days after asking Brad Karp about representing Misra and the same week Weingarten discussed the “Softbank caper,” Epstein emailed Eduardo Teodorani at CNH Industrial with a single line: “Allesandro benedetti?” (EFTA02628256). The 48-hour Karp–Misra–Benedetti inquiry sequence places Epstein as an active intelligence gatherer around the SoftBank scandal in the final months of his life.

sections.title: The Avenue Foch Connection
sections.content:
The documentary trail establishes Benedetti as a long-standing member of Epstein’s Paris network over an eight-year span from 2011 to 2019. The earliest evidence is Weingarten’s December 9, 2011 email to Epstein referencing “allesandro Benedetti, your Italian jewish neighbor on ave. foch” (EFTA00925685). The phrasing — “your” neighbor, not “a” neighbor — indicates Weingarten understood Benedetti as known to Epstein through the Avenue Foch property, the same 22 Avenue Foch that served as Epstein’s Paris base of operations. Epstein’s non-response to the Benedetti question in the email chain, while engaging on other topics, suggests either prior phone discussion or a deliberate compartmentalization of information about Benedetti.

By September 2013, Benedetti had been integrated into Epstein’s operational Paris network. Groff’s “Paris List” (EFTA02575400) placed “Alesandro de benedetti” first among fourteen contacts, a group that included Ariane de Rothschild, Wojtek Fibak of Fine Arts Investments, Margherita Campella Della Spina, a “Sultan,” and conductor Frederic Chaslin. The same day’s schedule (EFTA02297224) juxtaposed the Benedetti reminder with breakfast with Ian Osborne (the key Peter Thiel intermediary), lunch with Larry Summers, and a meeting with Richard Kahn and Darren Indyke. This day — featuring Epstein’s tech-intelligence contact (Osborne), policy brain (Summers), legal-financial controllers (Kahn/Indyke), and European network (Benedetti) — encapsulates the compartmented structure of Epstein’s operations. Duplicate reminders on September 26 and October 7 (EFTA02575276, EFTA02576024) confirm repeated scheduling around Benedetti during this Paris trip cycle.

The final documented contact comes on January 28, 2019, when Epstein emailed Eduardo Teodorani at CNH Industrial with the single inquiry “Allesandro benedetti?” (EFTA02628256). This terse, one-line question arrived exactly two days after Epstein had asked Brad Karp about representing Rajeev Misra and the same week Weingarten discussed the “Softbank caper.” The temporal precision of this Karp–Misra–Benedetti inquiry sequence — compressed into 72 hours — strongly suggests Epstein was actively tracking the SoftBank sabotage operation and sought current intelligence about Benedetti through Italian corporate channels. The use of Teodorani as intermediary rather than direct contact may indicate the Epstein-Benedetti relationship had changed character by early 2019.

sections.title: Corporate Architecture Across Jurisdictions
sections.content:
Benedetti’s corporate footprint spans at least seven jurisdictions — UK, Switzerland, France, Italy, BVI, Cyprus, and Malta — organized in layers that separate his public-facing advisory work from opaque offshore vehicles. At the visible level, he founded SAE Capital Ltd in January 2007 as his primary advisory vehicle and served as Chairman of Schwarzfield S.A. (from 2013) and Director of SPQR Capital Holdings S.A. (from 2010). SEC proxy filings for Equus Total Return Inc. (NYSE: EQS, CIK 878932), where he served as Executive Chairman from June 2011 to June 2014, provide the most transparent window into his portfolio: the DEF 14A disclosures list eight concurrent directorships and note personal ownership of over 100,000 shares plus 400,000 held through EB Finance S.A., an entity of which he disclaimed beneficial ownership.

The UK layer includes four Companies House appointments, each with distinct co-directors and corporate members suggesting different operational purposes. Asherco LLP (OC379532), active since October 2012, is the most revealing. Its membership has rotated through two BVI corporate members — Youngstown Investments Group Ltd (BVI 1688567, 2014–2021) and Satsu Finance Ltd (BVI 1583501, 2021–2023), both registered to the same PO Box 3483 at R.G. Hodge Plaza, Wickhams Cay 1, Road Town, Tortola. After the BVI entities departed, Israeli national Dotan Moshe (March 2023–July 2024) served briefly before being replaced by Mathieu Villaume of Luxembourg. This sequential rotation of opaque members through a single UK partnership is a recognized structure for obscuring beneficial ownership while maintaining a UK regulatory presence.

The Attali Investment Partners Ltd (UK 07138407, January 2010–December 2015) deserves particular attention. Named for Jacques Attali — former senior adviser to President Mitterrand, founding president of the EBRD, and head of Attali and Associates — it was co-directed with Bertrand Gauquelin des Pallieres (born November 1966, French, resident in Rome). Both resigned in December 2015 in the same month, replaced by Methorios Capital LLP as corporate director. The SIC code 64999 (financial intermediation not elsewhere classified) and the Attali branding position this entity at the intersection of Franco-Italian political circles and financial deal-structuring. Des Pallieres is separately identified as a former Deutsche Bank trader who worked under Misra and later introduced Misra to Benedetti for the SoftBank operation.

At the deepest offshore layer, Benedetti controlled Barkmere Group Ltd (BVI) — the vehicle through which Misra’s $500,000 payment was routed — and served as principal of Barkmere Limited (Cyprus). The ICIJ Paradise Papers confirm him as shareholder of Tree of Life Limited (Malta, C67345, incorporated October 2014), registered to Via delle Serre N. 9/A, Florence. A separate Cyprus entity of the same name (HE 279303, incorporated December 2010, dissolved January 2016) suggests a jurisdictional migration from Cyprus to Malta, with the Malta entity incorporated sixteen months before the Cyprus predecessor dissolved. This architecture — cascading from UK partnerships through BVI shells to Malta and Cypriot holding companies — provides layered opacity for financial flows of the kind documented in the SoftBank payment.

sections.title: The SoftBank Sabotage Campaign
sections.content:
In January 2015, Rajeev Misra — then a senior SoftBank executive positioning himself for leadership of what would become the Vision Fund — met Benedetti in London to commission a covert campaign against his internal rivals, SoftBank president Nikesh Arora and chief strategy officer Alok Sama. Bertrand des Pallieres, who had traded under Misra at Deutsche Bank before moving to Rome, made the introduction. By April 2015, Misra had paid $500,000 via Standard Chartered Bank to Barkmere Group Ltd, the BVI entity controlled by Benedetti. Misra’s spokesman later characterized this as an “oil investment” — an explanation that strains credulity given the documented operational timeline that followed.

The campaign operated on multiple fronts simultaneously. In Tokyo, an attempt to compromise Arora using women and hidden cameras failed when Arora did not take the bait. In parallel, Benedetti subcontracted Nicolas Giannakopoulos, a Swiss operative with ties to Cambridge Analytica’s parent company SCL Group, to distribute leaked banking records and establish a nominal shareholder campaign. K2 Intelligence was engaged to investigate Arora and Sama, and in turn hired Powerscourt Group, a London PR firm, to place the resulting findings. By September 2015, Giannakopoulos had hired freelance journalist Mark Hollingsworth, and in October 2015 The Independent published a story on Arora. The shareholder pressure campaign launched in November 2015 with the first formal letter arriving in January 2016. Arora resigned in June 2016. Sama followed in April 2019. The operation used the code name “Mr. West” for Arora, and Misra provided a dedicated cellphone for operational communications, with meetings conducted at London’s Bulgari Hotel and Zurich’s Hotel Baur au Lac (November 2017).

The operation unraveled because of compensation disputes. Benedetti had expected significantly more than the initial $500,000: a percentage of Misra’s SoftBank earnings and appointment as head of the Vision Fund’s London office. When neither materialized, Benedetti reportedly recorded conversations with Misra detailing the sabotage plans and ultimately leaked the full operation to the Wall Street Journal, which published its investigative report in February 2020. A Shearman & Sterling probe commissioned in 2018 proved inconclusive. The episode reveals Benedetti’s operational methodology — multi-layered subcontracting through intelligence-connected intermediaries, BVI payment channels, PR firm cutouts, and deniable shareholder campaigns — as well as his willingness to weaponize recordings when his principals renege on agreements.

sections.title: Epstein and the SoftBank Convergence
sections.content:
The most structurally significant finding in the Benedetti dossier is the January 2019 convergence that links Epstein’s pre-existing relationship with Benedetti to the SoftBank sabotage campaign. On approximately January 25, 2019, Weingarten discussed the “Softbank caper” with Epstein. On January 26, Epstein asked Brad Karp of Paul, Weiss about representing Misra. On January 28, Epstein emailed Eduardo Teodorani at CNH Industrial with the one-line inquiry: “Allesandro benedetti?” Three actors — Weingarten (legal), Karp (corporate defense), Teodorani (Italian intelligence channel) — queried within 72 hours about different facets of the same SoftBank situation.

This sequence raises the question of what role Epstein was playing. He was not, as far as the documentary record shows, a party to the original sabotage campaign. Yet by January 2019, he was actively gathering intelligence on the principal operative (Benedetti), exploring legal representation for the beneficiary (Misra), and discussing the broader “caper” with his own attorney. The possibilities range from Epstein positioning himself as a fixer or intermediary in the fallout, to gathering leverage material for his own purposes, to having had undocumented involvement in the operation from the outset — a possibility supported by the pre-existing eight-year Avenue Foch neighborly relationship. The fact that Epstein routed his Benedetti inquiry through Teodorani rather than contacting Benedetti directly may indicate a shift in the relationship’s character, perhaps reflecting awareness that Benedetti was now a potential liability or witness.

sections.title: Position in the Paris Network
sections.content:
Benedetti’s placement within Epstein’s Paris ecosystem illuminates the structure of that network. The September 2013 “Paris List” (EFTA02575400) is one of the few documents that maps Epstein’s Parisian social circle in a single snapshot. Benedetti appears first, followed by names that resolve to a mixture of European aristocracy (“Ariane” likely Ariane de Rothschild), art-world figures (Wojtek Fibak of Fine Arts Investments), Italian nobility (Margherita Campella Della Spina), Gulf royalty (“Sultan in Paris Sun. Sept 29th”), and cultural figures (Frederic Chaslin, operatic conductor). The list blends exactly the social registers that Epstein cultivated — finance, art, aristocracy, and Gulf wealth — with Benedetti occupying the finance/intelligence position.

His Attali Investment Partners directorship further anchors him in the Franco-Italian political elite. Jacques Attali represents the Mitterrand-era French establishment: former presidential adviser, architect of the EBRD, and a figure whose networks extend deep into European institutional finance. Benedetti’s position as a board member of Attali’s investment vehicle placed him at the nexus of French political access and Italian financial operational capacity — precisely the kind of cross-border bridge that characterized many of Epstein’s most valued contacts. His earlier role as president of M Finances SAS (Paris, 2000–2001) and director of Vendome Investments Limited (UK, 2005–2011) further establishes a Paris-London axis of operations predating the Epstein connection by a decade.
